### Format Educational biological illustration. ### Content Show a colony's principal nutritional inputs: - Nectar and honey as carbohydrate sources. - pollen and bee bread as protein, lipid, vitamin and mineral sources. - water for dilution, brood-food preparation and cooling. - supplemental syrup and protein feed as temporary management tools. ### Required qualities - Scientifically accurate worker-bee anatomy and hive context. - Clear distinction between natural forage and supplemental feed. - No commercial branding. - No implication that supplementation replaces natural forage.

### Format Professional decision chart. ### Decision sequence 1. Does the colony have a defined feeding need? 2. Is it queenright and otherwise healthy? 3. Is carbohydrate, protein or another management correction required? 4. Are harvestable honey supers absent? 5. Can the colony defend and access an internal feeder? 6. What quantity and concentration match the purpose? 7. Is the colony responding without robbing or brood restriction? 8. Has the objective been achieved? 9. Stop feeding and remove the feeder. ### Design requirement Use clean publication typography and standard decision symbols rather than ASCII artwork.

### Format Hive cross-section. ### Content Show a correctly sized protein patty positioned above brood where nurse bees can reach it. Also show: - Proper bee space. - small portion size. - inspection for mould. - removal of uneaten material. - small hive beetle risk in neglected feed.

### Format Step-by-step instructional sequence. ### Content Show: 1. Clean food-grade equipment. 2. measured water. 3. controlled warming. 4. heat switched off. 5. measured white granulated sugar added. 6. stirring until dissolved. 7. complete cooling. 8. labelled sealed container. Include separate examples for: - light syrup: one part sugar to one part water by weight; - heavy syrup: two parts sugar to one part water by weight. ### Safety details - No boiling syrup. - No hot feed placed in a hive. - No darkened or caramelised syrup. - Stable vessel and protected hands.

### Format Comparative cutaway plate. ### Content Show: - Entrance feeder. - top feeder. - frame feeder. - pail feeder. - bag feeder. For each feeder, indicate: - Colony access. - syrup reservoir. - anti-drowning feature. - likely leakage point. - relative robbing exposure. ### Composition All feeder examples should use the same hive scale and viewing angle where practical.

### Format Before-and-after apiary scene. ### Unsafe side Show: - Spilled syrup. - exposed comb. - wide entrance on a weak colony. - leaking external feeder. - bees searching hive joints. - sticky open containers. ### Safe side Show: - Internal feeder. - clean ground and equipment. - reduced defensible entrance. - fully closed hive. - sealed transport container. - prompt spill cleanup.

### Format Separated process illustration. ### Content Show: - Feeding phase with no harvest supers. - feeding stopped. - feeder removed and records completed. - colony reassessed. - harvest supers installed only after separation is confirmed. ### Message Supplemental sugar feed must not be stored in comb intended for sale as honey. ## Style Direction - Professional handbook illustration. - Natural honey bee colours. - Accurate hive components. - Clear visual hierarchy. - Legible labels. - Consistent perspective. - No cartoon anthropomorphism. - No manufacturer logos. - No decorative imagery that obscures instruction. - Suitable for both print and digital publication.
### Format Detailed technical illustration. ### Content Compare: - Float. - ladder. - mesh access. - roughened wall. - restricted access channel. Show bees standing safely above the syrup surface.

### Format Professional flowchart. ### Decisions - Is the colony alive? - Is it viable? - Are stores sufficient? - Are stores accessible? - Can liquid feed be processed? - Is solid feed required? - Is disease or queen failure present? - Is feed within cluster reach? - When should monitoring occur? ## Style Direction - Professional scientific handbook style. - Realistic honey bees and equipment. - Accurate seasonal conditions. - Consistent hive perspective. - Clear labels. - No cartoon anthropomorphism. - No commercial branding. - No decorative elements that reduce clarity. - Suitable for print and digital editions.

### Format Numbered instructional sequence. ### Steps 1. Assess weight and weather. 2. prepare solid feed. 3. locate cluster. 4. open only the upper cover. 5. place feed directly above bees. 6. restore insulation. 7. close and secure hive. 8. record and monitor.

Panels for rain-wetted supers, broken comb leak, chemical taint and brood found in harvest comb, each showing immediate segregation rather than blending.

Harvest lot → uncapping/extractor ID → shared pump transition → tank ID → recorded quantity → later storage/pack lot.

Knife, heated knife, fork, plane and commercial automated system, each with appropriate comb profile and principal safety/quality limitation.
Low-speed first side → turn → more complete second side → turn → finish first side, showing how reducing retained honey mass lowers comb stress.
Low-drop gravity flow and gentle food-grade pump versus splashing/high-drop turbulent transfer that incorporates bubbles.

Compare strong established comb with new warm foundationless comb under excessive force. Show factors: speed, heat, frame attachment and honey mass.
Extracted lot → quality check → settling → appropriate straining → controlled warming only if needed → documented blending/homogenisation if intended → identified storage/packing vessel.
Tank cutaway showing floating foam/fine wax, clear honey zone and denser sediment, with a covered lid and sampling/outlet points.

Source lots with weights/origins/quality data → blending tank → new blend lot → retained records supporting final origin percentages.
Glucose/water ratio, temperature, nuclei/pollen, seed crystals and storage history feeding into nucleation, crystal size and texture.

Crossed-out examples of flame, paper, thumb and water-spread tests with caption: physical behaviour is not reliable proof of honey authenticity.

Open versus sealed container in humid air, showing moisture movement into exposed honey and protection provided by a sound closure.

Tank cross-section during temperature change showing humid headspace air condensing on a cold lid and droplets falling toward the honey. Include mitigation through stable temperature and closed-container handling.

Sequence: liquid honey → fine/normal crystallisation → partial phase separation with crystal-rich lower layer and relatively wetter liquid upper layer. Highlight fermentation risk in the liquid phase.
Side-by-side panels distinguishing temporary trapped-air/wax foam from continuing gas, pressure and off-odour associated with fermentation.
Glass versus food-grade plastic: barrier, breakage, light, weight, heat sensitivity and closure integrity.

HOLD / RELEASED / REJECTED / REWORK ELIGIBLE examples with physical segregation and unique lot identity.

Incomplete corners, travel stain, propolis, pollen cells, brood evidence, leakage, crushed cappings, cross-comb, crystallisation, and heat-softened comb.

Bee escape, clean soft brush, cautious shake, and clean-air blower, with special emphasis on fresh wax fragility.

Side-by-side microstructure showing a few large glucose crystals in coarse honey versus many fine crystals in smooth creamed honey.
Conceptual sequence: supersaturated liquid → nuclei → many fine crystals sharing available glucose versus sparse nuclei growing large.

Sound base honey → controlled liquefaction of unwanted coarse crystals → cooling → fine seed addition → low-air mixing → filling → stable cool setting → finished smooth product. Label exact temperatures/seed rates as process-specific.
Magnified comparison of fine smooth seed, coarse gritty seed and partially melted/recrystallised seed.
High-speed vortex, bubbles and foam versus low-air mixing and short settling before filling.

Small seed/base premix being incorporated into the main batch with slow whole-tank circulation and no vortex.
Smooth set, gritty crystals, overly hard set, soft/unset honey, phase separation, wall frosting/streaks and fermentation gas channels.
Crystal-rich lower phase and relatively wetter liquid phase, with fermentation-risk caution.
Cappings wax, light honey-super comb, old brood comb, propolis-rich scrapings, and disease/chemical-suspect material shown as separate streams before processing.

Two-stage filtration removing physical debris, with a separate note that dissolved lipophilic residues/adulterants remain a chemical-quality question.
Clean mould fill → cooling contraction → normal central depression → underside debris removal → weighed/labelled block.
Cappings wax, light honey-super comb, old brood comb and contaminated/disease-suspect material shown as separate streams with different quality and destination decisions.

figures.working_title: New Comb Versus Old Brood Comb
figures.brief: Cross-section showing clean wax cells compared with repeated cocoon layers, propolis and brood debris. Include decreasing recoverable-wax fraction conceptually.

Apiary/source stream → treatment/disease history → rendering batch → block IDs → laboratory results/end use → buyer or internal foundation batch.

Stable indirect heat, temperature measurement, appropriate PPE, ventilation, clear floor, lid/fire-control plan and no children/animals in the work zone.

Hot wax/water/debris mixture settling into floating wax, water and dense slumgum layers, followed by solidified wax cake and dirty underside removal.
Two-stage hot-wax filtration removing physical debris, with a separate note that dissolved lipophilic residues/adulterants remain a chemical-quality question.

Pesticides, heavy metals, mould/mycotoxins, pyrrolizidine alkaloids, foreign bodies, and allergy as separate risk categories.

Paint, treated-wood fragments, plastic, dead insects, excessive wax, soil, mould, and chemical/fuel odour.
